analysis.one_liner: Raises fuel economy standards for light trucks, large SUVs, and the federal vehicle fleet.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to two House committees and a subcommittee in April 2003 and never received a vote before the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have raised the required average gas mileage for light trucks (pickups, vans, SUVs) in steps from model year 2008 to 2011, ending at 27.5 mpg. It would have expanded the definition of "automobile" to cover heavier vehicles up to 10,000 pounds, bringing large SUVs under fuel economy rules. It also required federal agencies to buy fleet vehicles averaging 3 mpg better than their 2005 baseline by 2007 and 6 mpg better by 2010.
analysis.who_benefits: Car and truck buyers, who would spend less on gasoline as the average mileage of new light trucks rose over four model years. Federal taxpayers would also benefit indirectly from lower fuel costs for the government's vehicle fleet.

how_it_helps.text: Light trucks would have to average at least 23.5 mpg in model year 2008, rising to 24.8 in 2009, 26.1 in 2010, and 27.5 in 2011, instead of the standard then in effect.

Vehicles weighing up to 10,000 pounds gross vehicle weight would be regulated as automobiles for fuel economy purposes, closing the gap that allowed the largest SUVs to escape the standards, effective January 1, 2011.
Federal agencies would have to procure new vehicles averaging at least 3 mpg above their fiscal 2005 baseline by September 2007, and 6 mpg above by September 2010.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, which would bear the cost of engineering and retooling to meet the higher mileage numbers, and potentially buyers of very large vehicles if the price of those models rose.

drawbacks.text: Higher mileage standards impose real compliance costs on manufacturers, which can translate into higher vehicle prices or slower availability of large trucks and SUVs some buyers and businesses rely on.
The bill set a single flat average per manufacturer rather than a size-based system, which critics of such mandates have argued can pressure makers to shift their mix toward smaller vehicles.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — lower gasoline spending for owners of pickups, vans, and SUVs and reduced oil consumption — are broad and durable, while the costs are borne mainly by manufacturers and spread thinly across buyers. The federal fleet provision is a low-risk efficiency purchase requirement. On balance the design is modest but sound; the main legitimate cost is compliance and the risk of higher prices for the largest vehicles.

outcome.mechanism: It got referred to two committees and then to a subcommittee in April 2003, and neither committee ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Wayne Gilchrest introduced the bill on April 3, 2003, joined by five original cosponsors from both parties.

The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Government Reform Committee, and on April 10, 2003 the Energy and Commerce side sent it to its Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality.
Twenty-four members cosponsored the bill, 21 Democrats and 3 Republicans.
No committee ever reported the bill and no vote ever occurred; the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 without further action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers, which continued to sell light trucks under the weaker standards in effect at the time, and buyers of very large vehicles who faced no new rules. Drivers paid for this in continued fuel consumption.

for.name: Rep. Wayne Gilchrest
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured 24 cosponsors.

for.name: Reps. Olver, Boehlert, Markey, Johnson of Connecticut, and Solis
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction, a bipartisan group.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, and never reported it out.

against.name: House Committee on Government Reform
against.what_they_did: Received the referral for the federal fleet provisions and took no action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican sponsor and 24 cosponsors split 21 Democrats and 3 Republicans, so it was bipartisan in support — but the obstruction that killed it happened in committee, where the record shows no roll-call to break down by party.

industries.note: The bill would have forced rising average mileage on their light-truck fleets and brought 10,000-pound vehicles under the auto standards, requiring engineering and retooling investment. Because the bill died without a vote, they kept selling under the weaker standards then in effect.
Agencies would have had to buy more efficient vehicles, raising purchase considerations but lowering long-run fuel costs paid by taxpayers.
